newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Labour bodies pledge trade link push, hit EU.
newsitem.headline: Labour bodies pledge trade link push, hit EU.

text.p: International labour unions pledged on Wednesday they would push hard for a firm link between trade and labour conditions in the rules of the World Trade Organisation despite a "sell-out" by the European Union.

They said they would be urging key governments to maintain pressure for a WTO "social clause" -- fiercely opposed by many developing countries -- to be on the agenda for the trade body's first ministerial meeting in Singapore in December.

And Marcello Malentacchi, current chairman of a coordinating body for global unions across a wide range of industries, said an EU decision to row back on its earlier strong support for their position was "a sell-out of the social clause."

"We will be working at the national level to keep up the pressure on governments to insist that the issue be raised at the ministerial meeting," Nick Grisewood of the Geneva-based commercial and clerical workers' body FIEJ told Reuters.
At Singapore, the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), a leader in the fight for a WTO social clause, would be running a parallel meeting on the issue.

The EU decision to avoid the labour standards issue in Singapore was taken in Brussels at a meeting last week of trade ministers of the 15 after Britain -- backed by Germany, Sweden and Spain -- argued it should be dropped.

Although divided, with France still arguing strongly for a WTO role, the ministers accepted the International Labour Organisation was the best forum for the issue -- a position also taken by many developing countries.

The four EU governments who argued for this stance and hailed its acceptance "should be required to explain how the denial of basic human and trade union rights in the newly- developing countries can be construed as a success," said a statement from Malentacchi, who heads the Geneva-based International Metalworkers' Federation.

"The liberalisation of trade is supported by the trade union movement, providing it is fair trade, but commitments to free trade are menaingless unless clearly defined guidelines are established which all countries must respect.

"Without such rules, and the means to enforce them, there is every likelihood of a return to trade wars and protectionism .... which harm everyone, particularly the workers, through lower living standards and increasing insecurity," he added.

The United States has made clear that it will not follow the EU, and suggested at a key WTO meeting last weekend that it might block agreement on the final agenda for the ministerial meeting unless the labour issue was included.
The two-year-old WTO's General Council meets on Thursday for a session originally intended to seal the agenda and a formal declaration to be issued by the ministers in Singapore.

But trade diplomats say differences remain so strong between developed and developing countries -- not only on the labour issue but also on environment and trade, on textiles and on investment and competition -- that accord is still out of reach.

At a meeting of the Group of 15 emerging economies in the Zimbabwe capital, Harare, this week, Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe accused the big powers of bullying them over trade and labour.

Mahathir, repeating the main argument against a WTO social clause voiced by many developing states, said the West wanted working conditions subject to trade rules to undermine the poorer countries' advantage from lower labour costs.

Western labour groupings, as well as governments, insist that this is not the case and that they simply want to ensure that trade advantage is not gained through gross exploitation of labour, including that of prisoners and children.

But wrapping up the Harare meeting on Tuesday, Mugabe said the group -- which includes major Latin American, African and Asian states -- had agreed "to resist any attempts to bring labour and other social issues under the umbrella of the WTO."
